podcast.title: Fred "Sonic" Smith's Death (1994)
podcast.body: Patty and Fred "Sonic" Smith remained married for six years after co-producing *Dream of Life*, until Fred died of a heart attack in 1994. This marked the end of their personal and creative partnership. "Patty and Fred remained married for six more years until Fred died of a heart attack in 1994."

podcast.title: 2019 Benefit Performance with Stuart Copeland
podcast.body: In 2019, Patty Smith performed at New York's Public Theater with Stuart Copeland of The Police and the collective Choir, Choir, Choir. This concert was a benefit to raise awareness for immigrants struggling at the Mexican border, where they performed her anthem "People Have the Power." The event was characterized as a "do-it-yourself happening," aligning with Smith's brand. "The occasion was a benefit to raise awareness of immigrants struggling at the Mexican border."

podcast.title: "Godmother of Punk" Still Performing
podcast.body: Patty Smith, often referred to as the "Godmother of Punk," continues to perform well into her career, almost half a century after her debut at CBGB. This demonstrates her enduring legacy and active presence in music. "As for Patty Smith, the so-called Godmother of Punk is still performing to this day, almost a half century after she made her CBGB debut."

podcast.title: Early Career - "Free Verse" Punk at CBGB
podcast.body: Patty Smith was identified as one of the CBGB artists in the 1970s known for her "free verse" style, distinguishing her within the nascent punk scene. This lyrical approach defined her early contributions to the genre. "to the free verse of Patty Smith"

podcast.title: Early UK Punk Performance
podcast.body: Patty Smith, referred to as a "punk priestess," played a show in England a couple of months before The Ramones' July 1976 appearances. Her performance was one of the few instances of US-style punk rock exposure in the UK before the Ramones' more significant impact. "Outside of a show, punk priestess Patty Smith had played a couple of months earlier, the Ramones appearance would be England's first proper exposure to US style punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Legendary Gigs

podcast.title: Marriage to Fred "Sonic" Smith
podcast.body: Just before the release of her 1979 album *Wave*, Patty Smith met Fred "Sonic" Smith, who was the former guitar player for the Detroit proto-punk band, the MC5. They fell in love and got married, and Fred later co-produced her 1988 comeback album, *Dream of Life*, which was their only musical collaboration. "Just before the release of WAVE Patty Smith met Fred Sonic Smith, former guitar player for the Detroit Proto-Punk band, the MC5."

podcast.title: Semi-Retirement in the 1980s
podcast.body: After finishing the 1970s with her *Wave* album, Patty Smith spent most of the 1980s in semi-retirement from music. She married Fred "Sonic" Smith, former guitarist for the proto-punk band MC5, and raised their two children in Michigan, just north of Detroit. "And Patty spent most of the 80s semi-retired from music, raising their two kids in Michigan just north of Detroit."

xref.title: Meeting and Formation (Sacramento 1972-1975)
xref.body: Erick perkaiser (Lux interior) and Kristi Marlena Wallace (Poison Ivy) met in Sacramento in 1972. They were drawn together by a shared passion for horror movies and record collecting. By 1975, they had formed The Cramps and began performing at venues like CBGB, sharing stages with bands such as The Ramones, Blondie, Talking Heads, and Patti Smith. "They met in Sacramento back in 1972, and were drawn together by their love of horror movies and record collecting. By 1975, they'd formed the Cramps and were playing places like CBGB alongside their hormones and blondie and talking heads and patty smith and so many others."

xref.title: Assault on Todd Smith's Girlfriend
xref.body: On December 5, 1978, while supervised by Rockets Red Glare at a club, Sid Vicious got into a fight using a beer bottle with the girlfriend of Todd Smith, the brother of singer Patti Smith. He was arrested, charged with assault, and sent to Riker's Island. "On December 5th, he went to a club under the supervision of Rockets Red Glare and got into a beer bottle fight with the girlfriend of Todd Smith, the brother of singer Patty Smith."

xref.title: Briefly Labeled "Punk" (Mid-1970s)
xref.body: In the mid-1970s, the term "punk rock" was thrown around carelessly, and even The Rolling Stones were, at one point, called "punks." "By the middle of the 70s, the term was being thrown around very carelessly, very liberally. Patty Smith was called a punk. And then so was Eros Smith and Bruce Springsteen, even the Rolling Stones."

xref.title: Early Performances at CBGB
xref.body: The Ramones were among the foundational bands that regularly played at CBGB by the summer of 1974. Their presence, alongside other emerging groups, solidified the club's reputation as a pivotal venue for the developing punk scene in New York. "By the summer of 1974, Hilly's bar, now known just as CBGB to everyone, was hosting not just television, but the Ramones, Patty Smith, Suicide, Blondie, Talking Heads, the Heartbreakers, and a bunch of groups."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Residency at CBGB
xref.body: Television began playing a regular Sunday Night Residency at Hilly Crystal's bar, which would soon become widely known as CBGB. Their performances, starting around the same time that displaced artists from the Mercer Art Center began migrating to CBGB, helped establish the club as a hub for new music in New York City. "By the summer of 1974, Hilly's bar, now known just as CBGB to everyone, was hosting not just television, but the Ramones, Patty Smith, Suicide, Blondie, Talking Heads, the Heartbreakers, and a bunch of other groups."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Female Pioneer Inspiration
xref.body: Kim Gordon of Sonic Youth is cited as an inspiration for the Riot Grrrl movement, representing a legacy of female pioneers in punk and post-punk. "Taking inspiration from the female pioneers of punk and post-punk, it would be Patty Smith and Susie Sue and Kim Gordon of Sonic Youth, Chrissy Hine, Oni DeFranco, and so on."

xref.title: Formation and Search for a Singer
xref.body: Garbage was formed by producers Butch Vig, Duke Erikson, and sound engineer Steve Marker, who specifically sought a female singer in the vein of Chrissie Hynde or Patty Smith, one who could sing in a lower register. "She was drafted into Garbage by three dudes, butch vig, the record producer, Duke Erickson, and another producer and sound engineer named Steve Marker."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90's Part 2B: Front Women

xref.title: Godmother of Riot Grrrl
xref.body: Patti Smith is widely considered the godmother of all the Riot Grrrls. She was a punk poet, author, and musician who first surfaced in New York City even before the punk movement fully took hold, releasing four significant and influential albums between 1975 and 1979. "But if there's a godmother to all the Riot Girls, it's gotta be Patty Smith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Riot Grrrls - A Primer

xref.title: Influence on Legs McNeill's "Punk" Fanzine
xref.body: The Velvet Underground were among the influential artists from the underground music scene on the "scuzzy side of Manhattan" that deeply resonated with Legs McNeill. His appreciation for such bands ultimately led him to establish the "Punk" fanzine, documenting this emerging musical culture. "Not only was he into the garage band music of the 1960s, he loved the velvet underground and Lou Reed and Patty Smith and the New York Dolls and Iggy Pop."

xref.title: Influence on Legs McNeill's "Punk" Fanzine
xref.body: Lou Reed was a pivotal figure on the "scuzzy side of Manhattan" underground music scene whose work Legs McNeill greatly admired. McNeill included Reed among the artists he celebrated and featured in his influential "Punk" fanzine, contributing to the definition of the burgeoning punk aesthetic. "Not only was he into the garage band music of the 1960s, he loved the velvet underground and Lou Reed and Patty Smith and the New York Dolls and Iggy Pop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Legs McNeill's "Punk" Fanzine
xref.body: Patti Smith was an artist from the underground music scene on the "scuzzy side of Manhattan" who inspired Legs McNeill. Her work, along with that of others, was part of the musical landscape that McNeill loved and documented in his seminal "Punk" fanzine. "Not only was he into the garage band music of the 1960s, he loved the velvet underground and Lou Reed and Patty Smith and the New York Dolls and Iggy Pop."

xref.title: Kim Gordon's Diverse Inspirations
xref.body: Kim Gordon drew inspiration from a wide range of female artists across different genres, including punk icons like Patty Smith and the Slits, Goths like Suzy Su, rockers like Joan Jett and The Runaways, blues singers like Billie Holiday, and her ultimate heroine, Tina Turner. "She was inspired by the women who came before her. There were punks like Patty Smith and the slits, Goths like Suzy Su, Rockers like Joan Jaden, The Runaways, Blues singers like Billie Holiday, and her greatest heroine, Tina Turner."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Last Words at CBGB Closing
xref.body: Patti Smith, an artist deeply associated with CBGB, appropriately delivered the final words on the club's closing night, October 15, 2006, marking the end of an era for the legendary punk venue. "And Patty Smith, appropriately, had the last words."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Morrissey's Hero and Name Inspiration
xref.body: Patti Smith, described as a New York poet, was one of Morrissey's heroes. Her name is cited as a possible homage or influence for The Smiths' band name, alongside the deliberate choice for a "plain" name and a Manchester nightclub. "It was also a homage to Patty Smith, the New York poet who was one of Morrissey's heroes..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Punk Pioneer
xref.body: Siouxsie Sioux of Siouxsie and the Banshees was a pioneer who took advantage of punk rock values, inspiring many to express themselves regardless of background or gender. "Suzy Su, of Suzy in the Banshee's, members of the Slitz, Pauli Styrene of X-Ray Specks, Chrissy Hinder, the Pretenders, Patty Smith, and so many more. They were all pioneers and they all inspired many people, women, but also men, to do what they did."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Record Deal and Distribution
xref.body: Blondie was among the New York groups that secured record deals, allowing their music to be distributed beyond the confines of New York City and reach a wider audience. "Eventually, word gets out and groups like the Ramones and the Talking Heads and television in Blondie and Patty Smith get record deals and their music begins to be distributed beyond New York."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
